title: Chapter 17 – Two Bells
html:
The lie goes out on the eighteenth morning, and it travels the way every lie in that house has traveled for ten years: inside a ledger.

Lin Jian watches it leave. He lies on the roof of the library with his cheek against a cold tile and a Moonlamp wrapped in cloth beside him, and he sees Second Uncle cross the courtyard at the hour of the second bell, soft-footed and smiling, a bound book under one arm. The book is the Patriarch's own household roster. Grandfather left it open on the council table last night, with the door ajar and no one in the room, and on its second page, in the old man's careful hand, are three sentences that were written for exactly one pair of eyes.

Patriarch unwell; fever since the funeral; keeps to his room. Full guard to the south gate for the Hundred-Herb Market, day twenty. North rim unwatched; quarry-gap pit flawed, pin six, repair deferred.

Every word is false except the last. Pin six is flawed. Someone flawed it.

Second Uncle stops at the library door. He looks left, then right, a small habitual glance, like a man checking his pockets. Then he slips inside, and the door closes, and Lin Jian counts. At two hundred and ten the door opens again. Second Uncle comes out with the book under his arm and a faint, absent, thoughtful look, and walks back to his rooms.

He has not copied anything. He has no need. He has a memory like an abacus.

On the latch of the library door, where Lin Jian dusted it with glow-salt an hour before dawn, a smear of pale light waits for the moon.

Day twenty, Lin Jian thinks. Two days from now. And he has read it.

He rolls onto his back and looks at the sky. It is going to be a clear day. Somewhere to the northeast, forty miles away across the ridges, a man with one good eye is also waiting for a clear day. Lin Jian does not know that for certain. He knows it the way he knows what a pin will hold: from the shape of the thing, and the numbers around it.

* * *

"Three hundred paces," says Old Hu.

He is drawing in the dirt of the forge yard with the tip of his rod, a rough map: the north wall, the quarry gap, the cedar-covered shoulder of rock that overlooks it. Su Qinghe stands at his left, arms folded, in her gray jacket. Grandfather has not come. Neither has Father. The fewer who know, the fewer who can be asked.

"Here," says Hu, and stabs the dirt. "The gap. The pit Wenhai tampered with. If the boy at the other end of this is any good, he's told his master that the north rim is thin, the Patriarch is in bed, and the only thing between him and the terraces is a flawed pit. He'll come that way. Anyone would."

"And the pit?" asks Su Qinghe.

"Stays flawed. We leave pin six exactly as it is. If he sends a scout ahead to look, he'll find what he's been told." Hu moves the rod. "This is where we're actually going to be. The cedar shoulder, a hundred paces up the rise. It overlooks the gap from the east. A man coming down from the ridge toward the quarry has to cross the shoulder first, because the other side is a cliff. That's where we put the real pit."

"With a dummy," says Su Qinghe.

"With a dummy." Hu glances at Lin Jian, who sits on an upturned bucket by the anvil with a ball of cord in his lap. "Which the boy has promised to make worth looking at."

Lin Jian lifts the cord. Beside him, on a square of oiled cloth, lies the thing he finished at three in the morning: a man-shaped bundle of straw, as tall as Hu, wrapped in Hu's own second-best jacket with a pinned empty sleeve and a broad-brimmed hat. In the center of its chest, sewn into a pouch of tight cloth, sits the spirit pith he took from the Walking Elm, a hard greenish lump the size of an egg that sings faintly with wood-attribute Qi.

It is a cheap trick. It is also the best lure he can think of. A blood-drinker hunts by the Qi he can taste, and old Hu's Qi is dense, earthen, stubborn, the sort of thing Gu Yan will have memorized across the width of a hollow. The pith will give the dummy a heartbeat. Not the right one, but close enough to pull a half-blind man across thirty paces in a hurry.

"And the eye," says Su Qinghe. "He lost it to pepper. He will have planned for pepper."

"He will."

"Then the pepper is a feint."

"The pepper is a hammer," says Lin Jian.

They both look at him.

He sets down the cord and takes a clay bottle from his sleeve, the stopper wrapped in wax. It is the same oil he separated for Father three weeks ago, but this is the last of it, ninety-one percent pure and much stronger than anything that has ever gone into a talisman.

"He'll wear a veil," he says. "Wet cloth, charcoal, oiled silk. Something that keeps the fumes off his face. That stops a burst. It doesn't stop a needle." He turns the bottle in his fingers. "Mother's Tidal Spear is water. If I thin it to a thread and put this in the water, the thread carries it. It goes under the skin. It doesn't touch the eyes at all. It goes into the blood."

Nobody speaks.

"He feeds on blood," Lin Jian says quietly. "Every time he uses the Draw, every time he burns his own to move fast, he's moving it through his body. If the pepper is already in there, it comes with it. He told himself it was only pepper, Mother. I think it's only pepper that can't be eaten."

Su Qinghe stares at her son. Her face is calm, as it always is. Then, very slowly, she unfolds her arms, and takes the bottle out of his hand, and holds it up to the light.

"Nine," she says. "How many threads can I carry in one casting?"

"Three. Maybe four, if you hold your breath."

"And where?"

"The thighs. The back, low, where the ribs end. Anywhere the blood runs close to the surface and he can't brush it off." He hesitates. "He'll feel it burn. He'll try to push it out through the skin. That is the part where he stops being careful."

A silence. The coals pop.

"Who taught you this?" Su Qinghe says. Her voice is very even.

"Old Hu," says Lin Jian.

Hu, who has been staring at the sky for the last several breaths, makes a small noise in his throat and says nothing at all.

* * *

They go out before dawn on the twentieth day.

There are three of them on the cedar shoulder, and a fourth who is not real. Lin Jian sets the straw dummy in the center of the pit, in a shallow bowl of gravel ringed with nine pins that Hu drove into the earth the night before: Hu's own, this time, real mid-grade spirit iron with a groove cut to the hair. Beside the dummy stands an anchor plate, a flat disk of black iron the size of a dinner plate, half buried. When Hu strikes it with his rod, the nine pins will wake together.

Su Qinghe moves through the ring of cedars to the lip of the rise. She settles into a crouch with her back against a trunk, and lowers her hood, and becomes part of the rock.

Hu positions himself on the left, in the shadow of an overhanging slab. His rod lies across his knees. His eye is shut. Anyone who did not know him would take him for a stone.

And Lin Jian goes east.

He goes a hundred and twenty paces down the slope, along a crack in the rock that splits the shoulder from the main cliff, a deep, narrow fissure, just wide enough for a boy to wedge himself into. At the bottom, on a flat ledge, he settles with his back against the stone and a cedar root across his knees. Two cords run from his hands, up the crack, over a lip of rock, and out of sight. One ends at a bronze bell under a cedar root near the dummy. The other ends at a second bell, far to the north, near the old stream.

He does not have to guess what is happening on the shoulder. In his lap, flat on his knees, sits a shallow bowl of water with a thin yellow slip floating on its surface.

Far-Sight Mirror. Father drew it in an afternoon and refused to say what it cost him. The slip's twin lies beneath the dummy, and the water in Lin Jian's bowl shivers, clears, and becomes a window: the cedar shoulder from above, bleached and silent in the gray light, with a straw man standing in the center of a ring of iron. He can see Hu's shoulder. He can see a hand's breadth of his mother's gray sleeve.

He wraps his fingers around the first cord, and waits.

It is the longest morning of his life.

The sun rises. The cedars warm and begin to smell of resin. A pair of jays squabble in the branches, then go quiet. Somewhere far off, a Lin guard shouts at a mule. Lin Jian sits in the crack with the cord between his thumb and forefinger and thinks about nothing at all, a trick Hu taught him, the long, slow, cold emptying of the mind that is not so far from a Level Two scan. He feels the weight of the Belt at his waist. He feels, against his ribs, the last Royal Spirit Chain. He feels the stone behind his back.

He feels, at the edge of his sense, forty paces out, nothing.

And then, at the third hour past dawn, something.

It is not a presence. It is an absence: a cold, wet patch of wrongness at the edge of what he can feel, like the place in a pond where a stone has gone through the ice. It moves. It moves with the soft unhurried stillness of a thing that has all the time in the world.

Lin Jian does not breathe.

In the bowl of water, nothing has changed. The dummy stands. The cedars sway. And at the top of the cliff, a hundred paces above the pit, a small gray shape detaches itself from the skyline and sits down on the rock.

* * *

Gu Yan has healed.

Not perfectly. Even at this distance, even in the pale mirror of a bowl, Lin Jian can see that. The man sits at the edge of the cliff in the Crimson Vulture Cloak, which has been mended in a dozen places with thread of a slightly different red, and his left shoulder hangs a little lower than the right. A leather patch covers the left eye. Across the lower half of his face lies a veil of oiled silk, black, tied at the back of the head. When he breathes, the veil goes flat against his mouth and puffs out again, slowly, steadily.

He is not alone in his stillness. At his hip, in a plain scabbard, rides a short curved blade.

Lin Jian's hand tightens on the cord.

Gu Yan sits for a long time. Then he takes something from his sleeve, a pinch of rust-colored dust, and blows it into the wind. The dust drifts down the cliff, glinting. Lin Jian watches it fall toward the cedars. It touches the leaves. And the leaves, very faintly, turn the color of old blood.

A survey, he thinks. He's reading the ground.

Gu Yan stands. He looks down the slope at the quarry gap. He looks at the cedars. He looks, for a long moment, at the straw man in the ring of iron.

He cannot see well. The patch has taken half his sight. But the pith in the dummy's chest is singing wood-attribute Qi into the air like a bell, and the jacket on the shoulders is Hu's, and the hat is Hu's, and the pinned sleeve is exactly where a pinned sleeve should be. Gu Yan tilts his head. He takes a single step down the rock.

And stops.

Lin Jian's heart seems to stop with him. In the water, Gu Yan's head turns, slowly, from the dummy toward the left, toward the place where Su Qinghe crouches in the shadow of the cedars. He cannot possibly see her. She is as still as the trunk behind her. But he looks anyway, the way a hunting dog looks at a bush where there is nothing to see and everything to smell.

Now, Lin Jian thinks. Before he decides.

He pulls the cord.

Far to the north, under a cedar root near the old stream, a bronze bell speaks once, sharp and clear and small.

Gu Yan's head snaps to the sound. The tilt of his shoulders changes. A man who has been sitting on his heels in a long, patient hunt is suddenly a man who has heard something at his back, and he turns toward it, one step, two, before he catches himself.

But the bell has done its work. It has placed a second watcher at the edge of his attention, a stranger in the north where there should be none, and in that moment Su Qinghe rises from the shadows like a ghost off a pond and takes three silent steps out past the line of the snare.

She is deliberately visible. She stands in plain sight in her gray jacket with her hood back and her hands at her sides, and Gu Yan's head comes round, and for the first time in his life he sees, in the full gray light of morning, the woman who broke his ribs.

He smiles. Lin Jian can see it in the way the veil moves.

Then Gu Yan pours off the cliff.

* * *

There is no other word for it. He does not run or leap. He simply loosens, like a cord coming undone, and the red mist rises from the folds of his cloak in a spreading cloud, thick as smoke from a green fire, and the whole shape of him dissolves into it and slides down the rock face in a long crimson ripple. It takes four breaths. In the bowl of water, Lin Jian watches the mist cover the hundred paces of cliff and cedar in the time it would take a man to run thirty, and flow toward the straw figure in the ring of pins, and gather.

He is not going for Su Qinghe. He is going for the pith.

The mist closes around the dummy. It folds over the hat and the pinned sleeve. Out of the red haze comes a hand, long and pale, and fastens on the straw throat.

Hu's rod comes down on the anchor plate.

The sound is not loud. It is a deep, flat, final note, like a gong struck underwater. The nine pins wake together. Lin Jian sees it in the mirror: a flash of dull red light running around the ring from pin to pin, closing like a snare on a rabbit's leg, and the gravel in the pit stops being gravel.

The earth drops. The ring of iron pulls inward with a long groaning sigh, and Gu Yan, still wrapped around the dummy, plunges to the thigh in a hole of thick, grasping, heavy mud.

He screams. It is not a scream of pain. It is a scream of rage, high and furious, and the mist erupts from him in all directions at once, red tendrils lashing, trying to carry him up out of the pit. But the Nine-Pin Pit is not made for the body. It is made for the Qi. Every tendril that touches the edge of the ring is crushed back into the center, and the mist thickens, and dims, and the gravel sucks.

Sixty breaths, Lin Jian thinks. Maybe seventy. Hu's pins are better than mine.

He lets go of the first cord. His fingers are shaking.

Su Qinghe moves.

She does not call out. She lifts her right hand, the fingers together, and the air around her fingertips goes pale and cold. A thread of water rises out of the dew on the cedar needles, a single bright line, too thin to see, and she casts it.

It passes through the mist as though through smoke.

There is a sound like a wet slap. Gu Yan jerks, once, sharp, as if a hornet has stung him, and clutches at his left thigh. A second thread. A third. They go in low, one in the muscle of the right thigh, one in the back just above the hip, one in the meat of the shoulder, tiny wounds, bloodless, the size of a pinprick.

He looks down at his thigh.

He does not understand. Lin Jian can see it. The man stares at a hole in his leg barely wide enough for a grain of rice, and nothing at all happens.

Then it does.

Gu Yan's face contorts. His hand flies to his thigh, and he claws at it, and a tiny trickle of pale, thin red runs down between his fingers. His breath hisses through the veil. The mist, the great red billowing cloud around him, shudders, flickers, and goes ragged at the edges, tearing away in streamers of angry pink.

It's in his blood, Lin Jian thinks. It's burning.

Hu rises from his rock.

For a man with one arm and a bad lung, he moves very fast. He crosses the twenty paces to the pit's edge in four strides, rod in hand, and his left palm opens, and a dull brown glow gathers in it like the light off a forge. Mountain-Breaking Palm. Lin Jian has seen him practice it only twice, on a boulder behind the granary, and both times the boulder split.

Hu strikes. The palm lands in Gu Yan's ribs.

There is a crack like a falling tree. Gu Yan flies out of the pit, tearing free of the grip with a spray of mud and blood, and slams backward into a cedar so hard that the whole trunk shudders and a rain of needles falls. He slides down the bark to the ground. His veil has come loose. One side of his face is bright red, the skin raw as if scalded.

For a moment, he does not move.

Then he laughs.

It is a wet, rattling, delighted sound. "Smith," he says, in a voice that carries clearly through the mist. "Hu Tieshou. I had hoped it was you."

Hu stands over him with the rod low and his palm still glowing, and does not say a word.

"Do you know what they tell the young ones about you?" Gu Yan coughs, and spits red. "That you were the finest hand the Veiled Forge ever raised. That you made the Sect's first Profound blade with your own fingers, and then ran away from it as though it had bitten you." He fumbles at his belt. "I never understood why. But I think I'm about to."

He draws the blade.

It comes out of the scabbard with no sound at all. A short, curved, ugly thing the color of old bone, with a nick near the guard that Lin Jian has never seen and knows at once. The edge ripples. Something inside it stirs and turns and begins, very faintly, to sing.

Hu goes white.

In the bowl of water, Lin Jian sees it happen. Hu does not step back. He does not raise his rod. He simply stops, in the middle of a stride, and his whole body locks, and the glow in his palm gutters out, and his one eye goes wide and fixed on the blade as if it were the last thing in the world.

The residue, Lin Jian thinks. His own blood goes cold. The blade is calling it.

Gu Yan rises. He is smiling again. He steps in, unhurried, and the curved edge goes across Hu's left side, just above the hip, in a long shallow slash that parts the jacket and opens the flesh beneath.

Hu falls to one knee.

"Mother!" Lin Jian cries, aloud, in a crack in the rock that nobody can hear, and the cord in his hand is already moving. He does not know what he is doing. He only knows that Gu Yan has turned his head to look at the north, at the sound of the first bell, and that a man who thinks he is being hunted from two directions is a man who will, for one moment, doubt.

He pulls the second cord with both hands.

* * *

The bell rings a long way off, high and brass-throated, three notes in a quick descending line.

It is not meant to fool a clever man. It is meant to fool a hurt one. Gu Yan's head turns, the whole shape of him tilts toward the north, and the singing blade in his hand dips a finger's width, away from Hu's throat.

Su Qinghe is already there.

She does not cast. She closes. In the mirror, she is a gray blur across the cedar needles, and her knife, the plain, short, rogue's knife that has hung at the small of her back for all of Lin Jian's life, comes out of its sheath and goes in under Gu Yan's raised arm, in the soft hollow between rib and hip, to the hilt.

Gu Yan screams.

It is not rage this time. It is real. He twists, the curved blade whips round, and she releases the knife and leaps back, and the edge passes through the place where her neck was. Blood sprays across the pine needles. He claws at the hilt in his side. His mist, what is left of it, goes out in a thin pink gasp, and he staggers.

Su Qinghe lifts her hand again.

The last thread of water goes through his thigh and into the cedar behind it. It pins him there, a hair-thin line of frozen blue, a spike of ice, driven through the meat of his leg and into the wood, and for a moment he hangs on the tree like a butterfly on a card.

Then he tears free.

Lin Jian does not see how. There is a sound like cloth ripping, and a gout of blood and ice, and the man pulls himself off the trunk, leaving a long red smear. He does not attack. He does not even look at the woman who stabbed him. He turns and runs, up the rock face, in a ragged cloud of pale, thin, watery mist, already fading, heading north-east toward the ridge, and she lets him go.

She does not follow. She is kneeling already, beside the old man, with her hands pressed to his side and her face as pale as the sky.

"Hu."

The old man looks at her. His eye is clouded and strange. "It's in the wound," he says, very quietly. "The blade. I can feel it moving."

"I know."

"It's the same. The same art, the same hand. It's in the cut, Qinghe, I can feel it—"

"Be quiet," she says. She tears a strip of cloth from his jacket and presses it to the wound, and her voice is flat and fast and controlled. "Be quiet and breathe. Jian!"

Lin Jian is already out of the crack. He does not remember climbing. He is on the slope, running, and the cord is still wound round his fist, and the Far-Sight bowl is slopping water down his chest. He reaches the shoulder and the sight of it stops him.

The cedars are red with blood. The pit is a crater of churned mud. The dummy lies on its back, its chest torn open, the spirit pith gone from the pouch. And Hu sits against a tree, gray-faced, with Su Qinghe's hands crimson to the wrist and a thin black thread of something that is not blood creeping out between her fingers.

"Run," she says, not looking at him. "To the gate. Your grandfather. The healer. Tell them Hu is hurt, tell them it is the blade. Go."

"Mother—"

"Go, Jian."

He goes. He runs ten steps, twenty, as far as the edge of the cedars. Then he stops.

On the rock face above him, running up the cliff toward the ridge, there is a trail. A long, ragged stain on the stone. At first he thinks it is red. Then the light shifts, and he sees it is not.

It is pink. Pale, watery, almost white at the edges.

Gu Yan is bleeding out the pepper.

Lin Jian stands at the foot of the cliff with the cord still round his hand and looks up at the trail, and thinks about a cave in the middle mountains that he has never seen, and a man with one eye who burns his own blood to run and cannot stop. He thinks about Hu's face. He thinks about the shape of the blade.

He's weak. He's hurt. He's alone. And in an hour, he will be a little less of all three.

He looks back once. His mother has her hands in the old man's side and her back to him. She does not turn.

He unwinds the cord from his fist, takes out the last Royal Spirit Chain, and starts up the cliff.
